standard.title: Perform music in informal settings
standard.description: sing and play music in informal settings
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can share arts works with audiences (AC9AMUFP01), understand the audience relationship, and have practised basic music performance skills (staying in time, using singing voice). They have not yet performed with formal introductions, staging decisions or post-performance reflection.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students sing and play music in informal settings, following agreed performance decisions, introducing performances to audiences, and contributing to post-performance discussion.

nodes.label: Following agreed performance decisions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can follow agreed decisions about how music should sound during a performance (e.g. using singing voice, performing at the agreed tempo, holding instruments correctly).
nodes.minimum_width: Follow at least two agreed performance decisions (e.g. use singing voice AND perform at the agreed tempo) in a group performance.
nodes.typical_width: Follow a full set of agreed performance decisions across singing and instrumental music — using correct voice type, agreed tempo, agreed dynamics, correct instrument hold; begin to self-monitor whether they are meeting the agreed decisions during performance.
wider: Discuss which performance decisions are most important for the audience experience — prioritise and explain choices
Practise a section of a performance specifically focused on one agreed decision, then perform the whole piece and evaluate whether the decision was maintained
nodes.hinge_reason: Following agreed decisions is the foundational collective skill of ensemble performance. Students who cannot subordinate personal impulse to group agreement cannot function in ensemble contexts, which underpins all performance work in Y3-4 and beyond. This is also where performance as a social and communicative act — not just individual music-making — is first established.

response_modes.reason: Agreed performance decisions need to be established early in rehearsal and reinforced repeatedly before performance. Consolidation here means using rehearsal time to practise the specific decisions — stop, name the decision, try it again — rather than running through the piece from start to finish.

success_criteria: Follows at least two agreed performance decisions during a group performance
Can identify whether they met the agreed decisions when reflecting after the performance

nodes.label: Staging and presentation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can make and justify at least one decision about how to position themselves in a performance space.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one reason why where they stand/sit during a performance matters (e.g. to see the conductor, to hear others, for the audience to see them).
nodes.typical_width: Contribute to decisions about how/where to sit/stand in a performance space — consider whether curved or straight rows allow them to see cues, whether standing or sitting affects their ability to perform accurately; try different options and discuss which works better.
wider: Try two different staging arrangements for the same performance and compare: which made it easier to see cues? Which looked better for the audience?
Discuss how the size and shape of a performance space (classroom vs hall vs outdoors) changes staging decisions

response_modes.reason: Staging decisions are a concrete, discussable case of performance planning. Use guided questions: 'Can you see the teacher/conductor from there?', 'Can the audience see you?', 'Can you hear the other performers?' This builds the habit of thinking about performance holistically rather than just about the music itself.

success_criteria: Can give at least one reason for a staging choice (related to seeing cues, hearing others, or audience visibility)
Contributes to a staging decision in a group performance

nodes.label: Introducing a performance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can introduce a performance by sharing information about the music — including at least the title and one piece of contextual information (e.g. who composed it, when or why it was created).
nodes.minimum_width: Introduce a performance with at least a title and one piece of contextual information about the music.
nodes.typical_width: Write or contribute to a spoken or visual introduction to a performance sharing: title, composer, and where/when/why the music was composed; deliver or display the introduction before or during the performance.
wider: Create a projected slide introduction for a performance — include title, composer, context, and one personal reflection from the performers
Introduce a performance by connecting the music to its cultural context — share one thing about where this music comes from and why it matters

response_modes.reason: Introducing a performance is a significant step from Foundation sharing — it requires students to frame their work in context for an audience. Support with sentence starters and a simple introduction template: 'The name of our piece is... It was composed by... We chose it because...'

success_criteria: Contributes to or delivers an introduction that includes the title and at least one piece of contextual information
Can explain why introducing a performance is useful for the audience

nodes.label: Respectful listening and post-performance discussion
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can listen intentionally and respectfully during others' performances and contribute to a post-performance discussion.
nodes.minimum_width: Listen respectfully during one peer performance; contribute at least one comment or question to a post-performance discussion.
nodes.typical_width: Listen intentionally during performances, participating where invited (e.g. clapping along, joining in singing); contribute to post-performance discussions by sharing what they noticed, what worked well, or asking questions of the performers.
wider: Ask a specific question of performers after a performance — e.g. 'How did you get your instrument to make that sound?' or 'How long did you practise that?'
Compare two performances of the same piece (e.g. a rehearsal recording vs the final performance) and describe what changed

response_modes.reason: Post-performance discussion integrates all previous performance work — following decisions, staging, introduction — with the audience relationship established at Foundation. Students who can articulate what they noticed connect performance as communication to their own listening experience.

success_criteria: Listens attentively during a peer performance without disrupting
Contributes at least one specific comment or question to a post-performance discussion
